name: Lahjty
tagline: Arabic dialect tooling: the name reads as "my dialect," and the product sits around dialect translation and practice rather than textbook Modern Standard Arabic.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Anything that is a dialect-aware prompt wrapper over a frontier model is a weekend build, and a decent agent will get you a working Egyptian/Levantine/Gulf switcher with RTL layout and a phrase deck in one sitting. What you cannot conjure is trustworthy dialect data: general models are strong in MSA, uneven in Maghrebi, and confidently wrong in ways a learner cannot detect. If the paid product ships native speaker audio, curated regional phrasebooks, or a tuned dialect model, the DIY version is a plausible-sounding tutor with no ground truth. Treat the build as a personal practice sandbox, not a reference. Our confidence here is low: this is a small product and the specifics of what it actually ships are thin from the outside.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app that takes English or MSA input, rewrites it into a chosen Arabic dialect with a transliteration and a short usage note, and saves keepers into a reviewable deck.
requirements: An LLM API key (Anthropic or OpenAI)
Node 20 and a browser that speaks Arabic fonts
Enough Arabic to sanity check output, otherwise you are trusting a guesser
whatYouLose: Native speaker audio and any real pronunciation feedback
Curated, verified dialect phrasing instead of model guesswork
Coverage parity across dialects: your build will be weak exactly where dialects are low resource
A mobile app and offline review on the commute
Someone accountable when the phrase you learned is wrong or rude
moatNotes: Dialect data is the whole game. Verified regional phrasing and audio is expensive to collect and cannot be prompted into existence.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because correctness matters more than features here. A dialect tool is only useful if you can trust it, and a learner has no way to audit a model's Levantine output. Paying for a product that at least claims editorial review, or that hired speakers to record audio, buys you the one thing your local build cannot generate: someone else's confidence that the sentence is right.
notes: Small product, thin public detail, so read the verdict as provisional rather than a ruling.
prompt:
Build a local Arabic dialect practice app. Single project, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable: Next.js 15 App Router with TypeScript, Tailwind, SQLite via better-sqlite3. One repo, `npm install && npm run dev` starts it on localhost.

Core loop:
1. A single page input where I type English or Modern Standard Arabic.
2. A dialect selector: Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf, Iraqi, Maghrebi, plus MSA as the control.
3. On submit, call an LLM (Anthropic Messages API, model from env) and return strict JSON: dialect_text, latin_transliteration, literal_back_translation, register (casual, neutral, formal), one short usage note, and a confidence field where the model must say low when the dialect is low resource.
4. Render the Arabic in a proper RTL block with a large readable Arabic font stack. Do not mirror the whole page, only the Arabic text blocks.
5. A "save" button writes the card to SQLite.

Review mode:
- A /review route that serves saved cards with a dead simple SM-2 style interval (again, hard, good, easy) stored in the DB.
- Browser SpeechSynthesis for playback if an ar voice exists, with a visible warning that the voice is MSA and not the dialect.

Explicitly in scope: local SQLite persistence, JSON export of all cards, a seed script with about 30 everyday phrases, and a banner on every page saying output is model generated and unverified.

Explicitly out of scope: user accounts, hosted deployment, payments, native mobile, speech recognition, pronunciation scoring, fine tuning.

Secrets: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and MODEL in .env.local, read server side only, never exposed to the client. Commit a .env.example.

Write a README that states plainly which dialects the model handles poorly and that this tool is not a reference for anything you will say out loud to a stranger.
